application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: To perform a schedulability test, scheduling analysis relies on a known, worst-case execution time (WCET). This value may be dificult to compute and may be overly pessimistic. This paper offers an alternative analysis based on estimating a WCET from test data to within a spec@ l e d of probabilistic confidence. A method is presented for calculating an estimate given statistical assumptions. The implications of the level of confidence on the likelihood of schedulability are also presented.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The traditional approach to scheduling analysis requires knowledge of an upper bound on the time taken for computation to take place to provide a guarantee of timeliness at run-time. There has been much work on improving the analysis of these systems particularly when they incorporate some of the more complex features of modem hardware [9, 12, 141. However this need for careful and complex analysis contrasts with many situations where only measurement of the computational process may be possible or economically feasible. What is required is a method by which these measurements can be used in place of a deterministic analysis. Given measured values for the computation time of a particular task it is possible to construct a model of the length of time that it will take for this task to complete its execution [ 2 ] . It is also possible to construct an estimate for the worst case execution time (WCET) based only on the sample of data collected for this model. Since this estimate is not guaranteed, it must have an associated confidence level. The advantage of this approach is that we are freed from the restrictive assumptions that can make the construction of an analytically derived WCET impractical.
'This work has been partially funded by the EPSRC, via a research studentship and supported by the assistance of the DIRC project and City University.

An attempt has been made to construct a process that will take as its starting point a set of sample data, obtained through experimentation, for each task. From these data a model is constructed for the computation time of each task based on a probability density function, a mathematical expression approximating the real behaviour of the computation time [ 2 ] . From a particular model an estimate of the WCET for the task from which the sample data is taken can be derived for any chosen level of confidence that is required. A range of methods for combining these disparate pieces of information into an analysis of a system of tasks are then shown. This allows a more accurate analysis than considering all tasks separately, as the likelihood of underestimation of WCET for any particular task is low (by the nature of the problem). Hence, for a system of tasks with estimates of WCET, or prior determined values of computation for each task in a system, a value is obtained that provides a statistical measure of whether the WCET estimates are sufficient.

div.head: Objectives
div.p: The WCET is an upper bound on the greatest time that a task will take to perform its execution when it has sole access to all computational resources and under the complete set of all possible environmental conditions. It is also important to note, for the purposes of this paper, that this particular value will be the lowest possible upper bound, and be assumed to be possible under actual execution, so that under repeated executions of the same task under random environmental conditions the likelihood that the WCET will be encountered tends to 1. The assumption that timely completion of all execution for a task is required necessitates the penalty that underestimation of WCET is a problem for correct execution of a system inclusive of this task. For this reason it is helpful to add an assumption that failure due to an overload of processor resources is a possible outcome of any form of statistical analysis. Failure due to overrun of computation on a particular task is just one facet of a greater problem of failure that includes environmental issues and needs to be approached separately from the scheduling problem.

The restraint that this work is attempting to overcome is the requirement to have certain knowledge of the WCET. This value can only be obtained from detailed analysis of the behaviour of a task and the system in which it is expected to execute. However in many situations this detailed analysis cannot be performed. An alternative approach must be utilised due to practical difficulties, cost constraints or to a level of confidence required in high integrity applications, which for each generation of hardware becomes more difficult to ensure. Measurement of the time taken for computation is useful, as it requires no knowledge of the task in question. However any value of WCET constructed from measurement will not be certain knowledge; any measurement process will, in general, fail to be inclusive of all possible situations. If measurement is to be used then this possibility of failure must be quantified. The topic of ensuring measurement is representative of the subject in question, both generally in statistics and specifically in the situation of measuring computation time is not the issue of this paper and will not be discussed here, allowing the statistical theory employed through the rest of this paper to be applied to a larger range of potential problems. The emphasis is on the theoretical aspect of the problem as opposed to the implementation to a specific situation, although some example scenarios will be presented in later sections.

div.head: Process of Investigation
div.p: There are three stages in the construction of a schedule as seen by this paper. The first step consists of a detailed explanation of the problem at hand and an outline of the techniques used to solve it, as shown in section 2. There then follows a brief explanation of the process of modelling of data, a subject that has been examined previously [2]. Both this and the establishment of confidence levels for WCET are explained in detail in section 3. The second step is the construction of a schedule, or the application of a schedulability test. This step is not examined; the subject of scheduling algorithms has been approached from many angles in established work that are applicable to this subject [I, 71.

The major part of this work is examined in section 4, that of the construction of a confidence level argument for the system as a whole. This work is concluded with a section as to how these techniques may be applied to wider issues in scheduling in section 5 and an overview of the presented results in section 6 .

div.head: Description of the Environment
div.p: Now that the rationale of this research has been established, the processes by which the estimation of WCET and establishment of a confidence for collections of tasks can be explained. In this section notation is given which will be used throughout this paper, together with an explicit declaration of the problem and how it is to be solved.

div.head: Notation and Task Model
div.p: Measurement and the sampling of data is a complex science, especially when there may be a subclass of extreme situations that can affect the success of modelling. There is an assumption that the measurement process is fair, which is to say; each test of computation time is assumed to be independent, the sample of computation times has been taken over a range of environmental conditions and the sample is of a size which allows generalisation to be used. The first and second requirements are conditions of the experiment while the latter is simple to achieve since this branch of statistics is usually applied to situations with sparse data. This given, a model for each task requiring computational resources in a system can be constructed. It is important to note that in this paper the value that is being modelled is not the execution time, but specifically the worst-case execution time. A system is defined as a set of tasks r = { T I . . . T ~} .

Each task will have associated with it a number of features, represented by the following notation which will be used in this paper. The deadline of T ~, typically dictated by the specification of the task. The greatest value in the sample of times from T~ The function representing the WCET of T,, a random variable. This statistic will be used to construct an estimate of the WCET. The estimate of WCET constructed in the process described in section 3. The confidence level with which the value of wi is held.

div.head: Defining the Problem
div.p: There are two problems that the process described can be used to solve. The first is to take a set of deadlines provided as part of the requirements for the system of tasks and the sample data and transform these into a set of estimates of WCET and a confidence with which the entire system will meet these deadlines. By writing E for the total confidence with which the whole system is held and xij for data item j of the sample for task ~i the above relationship can be written as:

div.p: The process described above is a three stage process. The first step is taking the sample data and using this to construct an estimate of the WCET, with a specified confidence level. The second step is to construct a schedule using the figures for WCET calculated previously. If the scheduling algorithm indicates that a system is unschedulable then there is the potential to recalculate estimates of WCET for lower confidence levels. The third stage is to take both the sample data and schedule and use them to calculate the confidence with which the system as a whole can be expected to meet all deadlines, E.

The second possible problem is of transforming a requirement for the reliability of a whole system, E and the sample data and producing a range of WCET estimates that will be ideal for producing a confidence of this desired level with the minimum use of computational resources and within specified deadlines. Then there will also be the possibility of using these estimates of WCET to perform a schedulability test.

As in the previous case, the raw data has to be used to calculate appropriate models of computation time. However, instead of calculating the value of ~i for a specific wi, the opposite operation is performed. (Note: it will be shown later that the relationship between w, and ~i is a 1-1 mapping.) The value of ~i for each task will be derived from the system confidence E and hence a suitable computation time estimate wi will be calculated. This can then be checked back with a required deadline. Both of these different processes are shown in figure 1.

Either of these techniques can be used as is seen fit, given pre-determined knowledge, and those unknowns that an experimenter seeks to find. The next step is to build the relationship between confidence level and WCET estimate.

div.head: Modelling and Estimation
div.p: It is necessary to describe the method by which WCET is estimated with respect to confidence level, and the models are introduced in this section. These models are chosen as being asymptotically correct for their chosen purpose, but they also exhibit useful properties which are important, not only for the model itself, but also for later stages when the information from a series of models is combined together. These properties are shown in this section and where appropriate, proven.

div.head: WCET Estimation
div.p: The statement that an observer is '99% certain' that an event will occur is often said in conversation with little evidence that this statement is a correct one to make. Statistics provides techniques to make an assertion, and to test to see whether this assertion can be made with any surety given the data that have been observed. This conJidence level is a value corresponding to the likelihood of a statement being true with the available evidence, and is very different from a statement of probability. For a prediction of WCET from statistical modelling there is a necessity that the value of prediction has associated with it a confidence with which that statement can be made.

When sample data are analysed, assumptions as to its underlying nature have to be made. These hypotheses can have testing applied to their veracity, this will lead to a confidence with which the hypothesis can be held. In a sense, confidence is a metric of 'belief' and it is subtly different to a value of probability. The probability of a statement S being true, say P( S) = p , is a mapping from the set of events onto the interval [O, 1 1 of the real line that says that given a number of instances of S , a proportion p of them are likely to be true, and hence an individual instance of the statement will have a likelihood of either being true or false in proportions p : (1 -p ) . A confidence is very different, and says that for a hypothesis with an associated confidence q, with which the evidence (i.e. the sample data and associated assumptions) indicates that the statement is factually correct in all instances with a probability of q. After the sampling of data only one fact is clearly known about the WCET of a task, it must be at least the greatest observed value, which is denoted max, for a task r2.

div.head: Probabilistic Model
div.p: A knowledge of the average timing behaviour of a task is not an answer to the problem at hand, that of the worstcase behaviour. Thus the model that is constructed must reflect, not the distribution of the computation time, but the expected maximum computation given that the value maz, will be the smallest possible value that the statistic can take. The model chosen to represent either or both of these facets of the task in question can be chosen from a wide variety of different statistical equations. If the underlying distribution of computation times, say X is described by the function F ( x ) = P ( X < x ) then the maximum of IC independent executions will be described by Fk((z) = [P(X < ( z ) I k . The particular model chosen is that provided by the Gumbel distribution [6], which by the Fisher-Tippet theorem is the limiting distribution for a random sample of independent observations which has no upper bound. The distribution of the WCET will follow the maximal model given the information that the value of the maximum will be at least max,. div.p: The above techniques are shown in an example program to illustrate how estimates of a fixed quantity, the WCET, can be constructed from a random data sample. A particular program with a known structure and behaviour yet variable execution time, due to the effects of superscalar architecture features in the processor, has its computation time measured. The program under observation has a single path and hence variation in execution time is not the result of control flow issues [2]. It was run 100 times, with a maximal reading of 963, a mean of 669.025 and a standard deviation of 143.378. Forming the approximation above yields a computational model with equation ( 5), all values correct to three significant figures.

div.head: Calculating WCET confidence to maximize system performance
div.p: Assume that tasks 71,. . . , T~ are ordered by increasing deadline. The likelihood that the first task will meet a deadline is P(B1 < Dl). The likelihood that the second task will meet its deadline will depend on the amount of time taken by the first task -if the actual WCET is less than the estimate then this time will allow an underestimation of the WCET of 7 2 to be handled given enough spare time. It must be emphasized that the times of the individual tasks will not be varying at all. In actual operation it may be that all tasks take far less than the individual WCET calculated to complete and correct execution will occur with time to spare with a far greater likelihood than is being estimated. At this stage, the only concern is with the WCET behaviour and the repercussions of using estimates of a WCET value, and hence all execution times of a task must be considered potential worst-cases. A useful early result to achieve is to value all tasks equally within the parameters we are allowed to vary. Given that these parameters are those of the statistical model chosen to represent the execution time of a task, the parameter that will have to be chosen is either wi, the WCET estimate, or ~i , the confidence with which this estimate may be held. There will be an upper bound on the value of w i , the deadline, although in general it will not be possible for every task to be assigned this maximum amount of computation. In general -the value of wi will not be given as part of the specification. This leaves the value of ~i to be calculated in the construction of a schedule. If there is a method of constructing an 'average' confidence E then the expected likelihood that the system will execute correctly at run-time, using the simplest analysis, will be o(n6).

An assumption made at this point is that information about the dependence of tasks and their importance are not known, or given as part of the specification, and that all tasks are independent in terms of their WCET, apart from the competition for resources. It has been established that a statistical WCET estimate can be constructed from measured data given a confidence with which this estimate is to be held. The values of these confidences, denoted as E , for task T,, are not given but must be chosen as part of the estimation process. div.head: Scheduling with WCET Estimates
div.p: The previous sections have established a method of transforming sample data into models of computation time for specific computational tasks, and how to develop these models into a process of forming a relationship between the estimate of WCET and the confidence with which this estimate can be held. Lastly it was shown that a schedule can be constructed by choosing an identical confidence in all of the tasks in a system. Now it remains to show how this analysis will combine with the information about scheduling in a system to allow a confidence with which a constructed schedule can be held.

div.head: Apportioning Computation Time
div.p: There are, of course, many different ways of scheduling a system of tasks. In this section we examine a simple scheme to emphasise the statistical implications over more complex scheduling issues. However the results presented are generally applicablewith the caveat that some details may have to be modified. We assume the non-preemptive execution of a series of tasks ( 7 1 , . . . , T ~} . The task sequence must be completed by a deadline, 0. This is exactly the scheme within a cyclic executive and is the basic behaviour of many other schemes. div.head: Calculating System Confidence
div.p: A model exists by which a task requiring computational resources can be represented as a parameterised function.

From this model it is possible to calculate the probability that a chosen WCET estimate is correct (confidence), or vice-versa. This allows a probabilistic assessment of a single source of uncertainty. What needs to be ascertained is;

what are the effects of a number of modelled tasks in a single system? If there is a system of tasks in a system with no slack in the schedule, what is the likelihood that the system as a whole will behave as expected even if the actual WCET of individual tasks differ from the estimates used in the construction of a schedule? A simple method of calculating the overall likelihood that the system will complete is to ignore the interaction between the two tasks and require that they both finish execution in the expected time. Under these circumstances the confidence level is the product ny=l E ~. For example if every one of n tasks in a system has a confidence level of 1 - then the confidence of the system as a whole will be (1 -lo-'))". For example for 10 tasks each with a computation time estimate with a 99% confidence level the lower bound on system level scheduling will (0.99)10 cz 0.904. As may be deduced this is an overly pessimistic approach. It is possible to exploit an important effect of the modelling procedure, that a WCET for a particular task is far more likely to be overestimated than underestimated. The result that is required, of this section of the paper, relates the confidences for individual tasks and the system as a whole. div.head: Future Work
div.p: When the requirement to have a known upper bound on computation time is removed then the ability to give a qualitative answer to the question of schedulability is also removed. Instead there will be a quantitative or probabilistic approach where schedulability can be seen as a possibility with a value of the likelihood that schedulability will occur with a specified time frame, such as the hyper-period. Alternatively schedulability can remain a fixed event and the confidence with which the evidence supports this view can be the metric used in the assessment of the system. Also, the analysis until this point has depended on the assumption of a single equal deadline by which all tasks have to complete all computation. This is a restrictive assumption to make and an adjustment to the analysis is required to create a method that is applicable to a greater range of scheduling problems. The following stage of research is to show that this technique offers the potential for improved scheduling of real-time systems particularly where the majority of the work performed is of a soft or firm real-time nature.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: This paper explains a process by which sampling the execution times of a particular task allows the construction of an estimate by which a value for WCET can be estimated. This value will either be dependent on the choice of the confidence with which this value can be held, or on the amount of time that is assigned to a task to complete its execution. Calculating estimates of WCET for individual tasks is useful. However the result that is required is not the likelihood that an individual task performs correctly, an entire system has to work within estimates to be acceptable. If all actual computation times Ci are less than or equal to the estimates of WCET, wi. then a system will be schedulable. This will provide a lower bound on -the likelihood of successful execution, but it will not take account of the overestimation of values for WCET cancelling out the underestimation that may occur. An important additional result is thus found, that the confidence required for a whole system of tasks is equal to that which should be chosen for individual tasks as long as the modelling process is fair and independent. The conflicts between tasks are investigated by starting out by examining the conflict between a task and those executing previously and then using the result of this to generalise behaviour for a greater number of tasks. The method examined is a simple method, which is still pessimistic, but provides a suitable lower bound for the overall confidence level of a system.
